1.title: Basic Network Security Concepts
1.text: Welcome to Module seventeen: Basic Network Security Concepts. It covers the exam area four point zero Network Security. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do seven things. four point one Explain the importance of basic network security concepts: logical security (encryption in transit and at rest, certificates and P K I, self-signed certificates, identity and access management with M F A, S S O, R A D I U S, L D A P (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), sam el, T A C A C S plus, time-based authentication, authorization with least privilege and role-based access control, geofencing). Physical security (cameras, locks). Deception technologies (honeypot, honeynet). Security terminology (risk, vulnerability, exploit, threat, C I A triad). Audits and regulatory compliance (data locality, P C I D S S, G D P R). Network segmentation enforcement (I O T and IIo T, S C A D A, I C S, O T, guest, B Y O D). Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: four point zero Network Security (fourteen percent). Exam format: up to ninety questions in ninety minutes; a score of seven hundred twenty on a scale of one hundred to nine hundred passes. Validated against: the official Comp T I A Network plus N ten to nine exam objectives, version four point zero.

1.title: Terminology and the CIA triad
1.text: Terminology and the C I A triad. The figure shows this: The C I A triad: confidentiality, integrity and availability.

1.title: Terminology and the CIA triad, continued
1.text: Terminology and the C I A triad. Confidentiality. Only authorized people can read the data (encryption, access control). Integrity. Data is not altered without detection (hashing, signatures). Availability. Systems and data are usable when needed (redundancy, D dos (distributed denial of service) defense). Threat. Something that can cause harm (an attacker, a flood). Vulnerability. A weakness (unpatched software, default password). Exploit. The method or code that uses a vulnerability. Risk. The likelihood and impact of a threat using a vulnerability.

1.title: Logical security
1.text: Logical security. Encryption. Data in transit (T L S, I P sec, S S H, V P N (virtual private network)) and data at rest (disk, database encryption). Certificates and P K I. A public key infrastructure issues certificates signed by a certificate authority to prove identity and enable encryption; self-signed certificates are not trusted by default (testing, internal use). M F A. Two or more factors: something you know, have, are. S S O. One sign-in for many applications. R A D I U S. Centralized authentication for network access (Wi-Fi, V P N, eight oh two dot one X); U D P, encrypts only the password. T A C A C S plus. Centralized authentication and authorization for device administration; T C P, encrypts the whole payload; separates authentication, authorization and accounting.

1.title: Logical security, continued
1.text: Logical security. L D A P. Directory access (three hundred eighty-nine; L D A P S six hundred thirty-six). sam el. X M L-based federation for web S S O between an identity provider and a service. Time-based authentication. Access is allowed only at certain times, or time-based one-time passwords. Authorization. What an authenticated user may do: least privilege, role-based access control (R B A C). Geofencing. Access depends on physical location. Exam tip: R A D I U S equals network access (users). T A C A C S plus equals device administration (admins) and encrypts the full payload. A self-signed certificate is not trusted by browsers.

1.title: Physical security and deception
1.text: Physical security and deception. Cameras, locks. Detect and deter physical access (badges, rack locks, mantraps). Honeypot. A decoy system that attracts attackers so you can study and detect them. Honeynet. A decoy network of honeypots.

1.title: Compliance and segmentation
1.text: Compliance and segmentation. Data locality. Where data is stored must follow legal rules. P C I D S S. Payment card data security standard. G D P R. E U personal data privacy regulation. Network segmentation enforcement. Separate devices by risk with V L A Ns, firewalls and A C Ls: I O T and IIo T devices, S C A D A or I C S or O T systems (industrial control, keep isolated), guest, B Y O D. Exam tip: I O T, industrial control and guest devices belong in their own segments, away from sensitive systems. Exam tip: R A D I U S authenticates network access; T A C A C S plus administers devices and encrypts the full payload.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Network administrators must be authenticated and authorized per command on switches, with the full payload encrypted. Which protocol fits? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: T A C A C S plus. T A C A C S plus is used for device administration and encrypts the whole payload.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Wireless users must authenticate through eight oh two dot one X against a central server. Which protocol is typically used? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: R A D I U S. R A D I U S provides network access authentication.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. An unpatched web server is exposed to the internet. What does the unpatched flaw represent? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: A vulnerability. A weakness is a vulnerability; the attacker's code is the exploit.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A security team deploys a decoy server to learn how attackers behave. What is it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: A honeypot. Honeypots are decoys to attract and study attackers.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A factory's industrial control systems must be protected from the corporate and guest networks. What should be implemented? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Network segmentation with strict firewall rules. Segmentation isolates O T and I C S systems.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Which certificate type is not trusted by browsers by default? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: A self-signed certificate. Self-signed certificates have no trusted issuer.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What does the C I A triad stand for? Answer: Confidentiality, integrity and availability. Question two. What is the difference between a vulnerability and an exploit? Answer: A vulnerability is a weakness; an exploit uses it. Question three. Which protocol encrypts the entire payload, R A D I U S or T A C A C S plus? Answer: T A C A C S plus.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What is a honeynet? Answer: A decoy network of honeypots. Question five. What does sam el provide? Answer: Federated web single sign-on. Question six. Which regulation covers payment card data? Answer: P C I D S S.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Terms: C I A; threat, vulnerability, exploit, risk. A A A tools: R A D I U S (network access, U D P), T A C A C S plus (device admin, T C P, full encryption), L D A P, sam el, M F A, S S O. Authorization: least privilege, R B A C, geofencing, time-based. Other: P K I and self-signed, honeypot and honeynet, P C I D S S, G D P R, data locality, segmentation of I O T, O T, guest, B Y O D.
